 Inappropriate Antibiotic Prescribing for Dengue Cost Singapore Millions Over a Decade

 November 21, 2026

 Reading Time: 7 mins read

 Inappropriate Antibiotic Prescribing for Dengue Cost Singapore Millions Over a Decade
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 A decision tree modeling study evaluating healthcare surveillance data in Singapore found that inappropriate antibiotic prescribing for laboratory-confirmed dengue cases from 2015 through 2024 generated an estimated cumulative economic burden of 14.32 million Singapore dollars from a healthcare system perspective and 16.13 million Singapore dollars from a societal perspective, expressed in 2025 values. Dengue is an acute viral disease for which antibacterial therapies are clinically ineffective, yet early systemic clinical manifestations such as fever, rash, myalgia, headache, and sore throat frequently mirror acute bacterial infections. This diagnostic overlap, combined with delays or incomplete deployment of diagnostic assays during initial patient encounters, leads healthcare practitioners to empirically initiate antibacterial agents before a definitive viral etiology is established. The retrospective analysis was specifically structured to quantify the clinical volume and economic consequences of unnecessary antibacterial therapy across both inpatient and ambulatory healthcare delivery sectors, applying local clinical cohort prescribing benchmarks to national notification registries.
 The underlying epidemiological burden of dengue remains a persistent public health challenge in Singapore, where the infection is endemic with continuous year-round transmission and substantial epidemic cyclicality driven by complex vector ecology, serotype switching, and climatic fluctuations. During the ten-year evaluation window, national surveillance recorded notable outbreak peaks where annual notifications exceeded 30,000 cases, specifically during epidemic surges observed in 2020 and 2022. Across the entirety of the 2015 to 2024 analytical period, the Ministry of Health Singapore documented a cumulative total of 142,525 laboratory-confirmed cases. While vector mitigation programs and public health infrastructure maintain robust surveillance, the constant presentation of large numbers of febrile individuals into primary and tertiary care environments creates an ongoing clinical challenge. In outpatient facilities where consultation times are constrained and rapid point-of-care confirmation is not universally deployed, clinicians frequently manage undifferentiated fever under diagnostic uncertainty, inadvertently fostering antibacterial overuse despite broader national initiatives targeting antimicrobial stewardship.
 To model patient movement and clinical decision points across the healthcare system, the investigators developed a comprehensive decision tree framework using R software version 4.3.3. The total population of 142,525 notified cases was initially stratified into inpatient and outpatient care pathways based on a national hospitalisation proportion of 37.1 percent, resulting in 52,877 hospitalised patients and 89,648 ambulatory cases. The decision tree traced patients across 14 discrete terminal branches defined by diagnostic testing status, testing accuracy, the subsequent acquisition of hospital-acquired bacterial infections, and the empirical prescription of antibacterial therapy. Within this tree architecture, five terminal branches captured inappropriate antibiotic prescribing, defined specifically as antibiotic administration to patients with confirmed dengue infection in the absence of secondary hospital-acquired infections, reflecting clinical scenarios where antibacterial administration offered no therapeutic benefit.
 Model parameter inputs were derived predominantly from local clinical datasets and peer-reviewed literature to preserve context-specific accuracy. For hospitalised individuals, the empirical antibiotic prescription rate was assigned as 3.0 percent, drawn directly from observations in the Prospective Adults Dengue Study where 15 out of 499 polymerase chain reaction-confirmed patients received antibacterial drugs. For ambulatory patients, prescribing behavior was parameterized using the Early DENgue cohort, in which 6.1 percent of laboratory-confirmed patients received antibiotics. In the ambulatory branch, the proportion of practitioners utilizing diagnostic assays was set at 56 percent based on primary care practice surveys, with NS1 antigen diagnostic test sensitivity established at 89 percent. Hospitalised patients were assumed to undergo universal diagnostic testing, while the incidence of hospital-acquired infections among admitted patients was estimated at 11.9 percent based on multi-center inpatient surveillance data, ensuring that antibacterial use justified by nosocomial secondary complications was excluded from the inappropriate category.
 Applying these decision pathways across the ten-year caseload yielded an estimated total of 7,055 antibiotic prescriptions, of which 6,866 met the study criteria for inappropriate prescribing. The vast majority of these unwarranted prescriptions originated in ambulatory care settings, which accounted for 5,469 prescriptions or 79.6 percent of all inappropriate antibacterial use. In contrast, hospitalised inpatient cohorts accounted for 1,397 inappropriate prescriptions. The high concentration of unnecessary prescriptions in the outpatient sector highlights that primary care clinics, which manage nearly two-thirds of all dengue presentations, represent the primary setting where initial clinical uncertainty and variable testing practices drive non-indicated empirical prescribing. Hospital inpatient environments accounted for a smaller proportion of prescription events due to higher baseline testing rates, greater diagnostic oversight, and established hospital-based antimicrobial stewardship programs.
 The economic burden assessment captured direct medical expenses, direct non-medical expenses, and indirect productivity losses, standardizing all financial metrics to 2025 Singapore dollars using official healthcare consumer price indices. The cumulative societal cost burden of 16.13 million Singapore dollars corresponds to an annualized societal expenditure of approximately 1.61 million dollars, while the healthcare system burden of 14.32 million dollars represents an average annual cost of 1.43 million dollars. Direct medical expenditures constituted the vast majority of total costs, totaling 14.32 million dollars. Within direct medical costs, prolonged hospital stays resulting from antibiotic complications formed the largest individual cost driver at 10.11 million dollars, followed by direct management of adverse drug events at 3.26 million dollars and baseline antibiotic acquisition costs at 0.95 million dollars. Direct non-medical costs, reflecting informal caregiving time, totaled 1.00 million dollars, while patient productivity losses contributed an additional 0.81 million dollars.
 Unit cost allocations reflected substantial differences across healthcare tiers and the compounding impact of iatrogenic complications. Baseline antibiotic acquisition costs were estimated at 4.74 Singapore dollars per course in public polyclinics, rising to 55.35 dollars in private general practice clinics and reaching 502.72 dollars per treatment course within inpatient hospital wards. For individuals experiencing adverse drug reactions, direct management expenditures averaged 881.17 dollars per hospitalised patient and 371.09 dollars for ambulatory patients whose reactions necessitated emergency department evaluation or hospital admission. Furthermore, patients suffering adverse reactions were modeled to experience extended hospitalisations averaging two additional inpatient days, adding 7,235.92 dollars in direct bed-day expenses. Indirect productivity losses and informal caregiving valuations were estimated using Singapore median wage statistics under the human capital approach, calculating two lost working days for prolonged inpatient admissions and four lost days for severe outpatient adverse reactions.
 To evaluate parameter stability and pinpoint the factors driving financial variability, the authors executed a one-way deterministic sensitivity analysis by varying seven key clinical and economic inputs across their empirical upper and lower bounds. The resulting tornado diagram demonstrated that the antibiotic prescribing rates in both hospital and ambulatory settings exerted the strongest influence on total economic burden. Altering the hospital-based antibiotic prescribing rate from 1.0 percent to 31.0 percent shifted the cumulative economic estimate from 7.33 million to 139.33 million Singapore dollars relative to the 16.13 million base case. Similarly, varying the ambulatory prescribing rate between 3.0 percent and 74.6 percent produced total costs ranging from 14.64 million to 49.03 million dollars. Secondary sensitivity drivers included overall hospitalisation proportions, which varied total costs from 5.59 million to 33.48 million dollars, and prolonged inpatient bed costs, which caused fluctuations between 11.07 million and 26.23 million dollars, whereas hospital-acquired infection rates and inpatient adverse event treatment costs generated minor variations under 1.2 million dollars each.
 The investigators also conducted a probabilistic sensitivity analysis utilizing Monte Carlo simulation with 10,000 iterations to quantify joint parameter uncertainty across 17 epidemiological, clinical, and economic variables simultaneously. Probabilities and proportions were modeled using bounded beta distributions, while financial and cost parameters were assigned right-skewed gamma distributions to capture wide observational variances. Across the 10,000 simulations, total estimated societal costs ranged from a minimum of 0.87 million Singapore dollars to a maximum of 136.71 million dollars. The resulting cost distribution displayed pronounced right skewness, yielding a simulation mean of 16.16 million Singapore dollars and a median value of 12.94 million dollars. The 95 percent uncertainty interval, spanning the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentiles of the simulated outcomes, extended from 2.78 million to 49.60 million dollars, confirming that while most simulated scenarios cluster around lower expenditure bands, a non-negligible potential for substantial economic loss exists when high prescribing rates coincide with adverse clinical courses.
 Placing these economic figures within the broader landscape of public health expenditures reveals that the financial footprint of inappropriate prescribing in dengue is comparable to other major disease burdens in Singapore. For example, annual acute care costs attributable to carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales nosocomial infections in Singapore have been documented at 12.16 million to 12.33 million dollars, while the total annual societal burden of foodborne pathogens was estimated at 15.10 million dollars in 2019. Furthermore, the ten-year cumulative preventable burden of 16.13 million dollars approaches the landmark 20 million dollar investment allocated by the Ministry of Health in 2011 to establish hospital-based antimicrobial stewardship programs and computerized clinical decision support systems, demonstrating that inappropriate prescribing within a single viral infection can offset substantial public investments in stewardship infrastructure.
 Regional comparisons across Southeast and East Asia suggest that the absolute economic burden documented in Singapore may be substantially magnified in neighboring territories characterized by larger caseloads and higher empirical prescription rates. Epidemiological studies from Taiwan documented that 24.6 percent of confirmed adult dengue patients received antibacterial prescriptions within the clinical evaluation window, encompassing 6.1 percent of outpatient presentations and 30.1 percent of inpatient admissions. Cohort data from Thailand identified an inpatient antibiotic prescribing rate of 9.3 percent, while outbreak reports from Pakistan recorded antibiotic use in 47 out of 68 confirmed dengue cases. When compared to regional disease volume across Southeast Asia, where annual dengue episodes are estimated at 2.9 million cases, these higher baseline prescribing proportions indicate that the systemic financial loss and selective pressure for antimicrobial resistance across the region far exceed the levels quantified within Singapore’s relatively tightly monitored healthcare system.
 Beyond immediate healthcare consumption, inappropriate antibiotic therapy accelerates antimicrobial resistance by exerting selective evolutionary pressure on bacterial populations, leading to resistant pathogen strains that increase future clinical mortality and clinical management costs. While the primary decision tree did not model dynamic, long-term resistance epidemiology, the authors conducted an illustrative calculation assuming a 7 percent incidence of drug-resistant infections among the 6,866 inappropriately treated patients. At an average management cost of 9,913 dollars per resistant infection episode, this pathway would generate approximately 481 resistant infections, adding an estimated 4.76 million dollars in downstream healthcare expenditures. Because this downstream dynamic was excluded from the formal base-case calculation alongside long-term microbiome disruption, the primary findings likely represent a conservative estimate of the true societal and clinical damage attributable to unnecessary prescribing.
 The study authors identified several structural limitations inherent to their modeling design that frame the interpretation of the results. First, the decision tree framework was static and relied on the assumption of independence between hospital-acquired infection status and antibacterial prescription, creating a modeled subgroup of 5,438 dengue patients with nosocomial infections who did not receive antibiotics, which reflects modeling structure rather than untreated clinical disease. Second, key baseline clinical behaviors were parameterized using historical cohort studies such as EDEN and PADS, which, despite offering detailed local data, may not fully mirror evolving modern prescribing patterns. Third, lack of age-stratified data prevented the researchers from isolating vulnerable elderly demographics who frequently encounter higher antibiotic exposure, and the human capital approach applied to productivity loss may overestimate true economic disruption by assuming every lost working hour translates directly into unrecoverable societal output. Addressing these data gaps through dynamic epidemiological models and updated prescribing registries will be necessary to refine targeted stewardship interventions across the primary care sector.
 Subject of Research: Economic burden of inappropriate antibiotic prescribing attributable to dengue in Singapore
 Article Title: Economic Burden of Inappropriate Antibiotic Prescribing Attributable to Dengue in Singapore
